questions.stem_latex: In early planetary models, planets orbit the sun in circular orbits. Suppose a planet completes its orbit of radius $r$ around the sun in time $T$, while moving at a constant speed $v$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

$$\text{constant speed}=\frac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time}}.$$

parts.label: b

questions.stem_latex: A patient is undergoing a treatment involving repeated injections of $M$ milliliters of medicine, separated by regular time intervals of $t$ hours. Let $A_n$ be the amount of medicine in the body immediately after the $n^{\text{th}}$ injection, so $A_1=M$. While in the body, the medicine decays exponentially such that the amount left in the body right before the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ injection is given by $A_ne^{-t}$.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

questions.stem_latex:

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} \hline & \text{Monday} & \text{Tuesday} & \text{Wednesday} & \text{Thursday} & \text{Friday} \\ \hline \text{Week 1} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} \\ \text{Week 2} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} \\ \text{Week 3} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} \\ \text{Week 4} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} \\ \text{Week 5} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{A} \\ \text{Week 6} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} \\ \text{Week 7} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} \\ \hline & & & \vdots & & \\ \hline \text{Week 36} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} \\ \text{Week 37} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} \\ \text{Week 38} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} \\ \text{Week 39} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} \\ \text{Week 40} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{A} & \text{B} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$f(x)=\sin x^3$ is an odd function so $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\sin x^3\,dx=0$

$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}e^x\,dx=\Big[e^x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=e-\frac{1}{e}=2.35\cdots$

$f(x)=\dfrac{e^{x^2}}{2}$ is an even function, so $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{e^{x^2}}{2}\,dx=\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx$

$\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^x\,dx$ as $x^2\le x$ for $0\le x\le 1$

$\displaystyle\therefore\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{e^{x^2}}{2}\,dx\le\Big[e^x\Big]_0^1=e-1=1.71\cdots$

solutions.latex:
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{2}{t+1}-1\,dt$

$=\Big[2\ln|t+1|-t\Big]_0^1$

$=2\ln 2-1$

As $a<0$ for all $t$, and $v=0$ when $t=1$, the velocity will be negative after $t=1$

so the distance travelled in the next second will be given by:

$\Big[t-2\ln|t+1|\Big]_1^2$

$=2-2\ln 3-(1-2\ln 2)$

$=1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$

total distance is given by:

$2\ln 2-1+1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$

$=4\ln 2-2\ln 3$

$=\ln 2^4-\ln 3^2$

$=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)$

$\therefore\ b=\dfrac{16}{9}$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct value $b=\dfrac{16}{9}$; 2: Also finds distance $1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$ for $1\le t\le 2$; 1: Distance $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$

$u=x\qquad v=\sin x$

$u'=1\qquad v'=\cos x$

$\dfrac{d}{dx}\,x\sin x=\sin x+x\cos x$

$\displaystyle\int\sin x+x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x$

$\displaystyle\int\sin x\,dx+\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x$

$\displaystyle -\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x$

$\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x+\cos x+C$

$r^3=kT^2$

$\dfrac{1}{T^2}=\dfrac{k}{r^3}$

$\dfrac{1}{T}=\dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{r^{3/2}}$

Substituting this into part (a) we get:

$v=2\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-1/2}$

$\dfrac{dv}{dr}=-\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-3/2}$

$\dfrac{dv}{dr}=-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{k}}{r\sqrt{r}}$

$\therefore\ \dfrac{dv}{dr}$ is always negative for $r>0$

$\therefore\ v(r)$ is a decreasing function for $r>0$, therefore planets further away move slower
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct conclusion; right conclusion based on correct derivative for last mark; 1: Obtains $v=2\pi\sqrt{k}\,r^{-1/2}$

solutions.latex:
Since $A_n$ is an increasing function in $n$, we need to consider $A_\infty$ for treatment to always be safe

$A_\infty$ exists as $0<e^{-t}<1$ for $t\ge 0$

$A_\infty=M(1+e^{-t}+e^{-2t}+e^{-3t}+\cdots)$

$A_\infty=M\times\dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}}$

$A_\infty=\dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}}$

We require $A_\infty<2M$

$\dfrac{M}{1-e^{-t}}<2M$

$\dfrac{1}{1-e^{-t}}<2$

$\dfrac{e^t}{e^t-1}<2$

$e^t<2e^t-2$

$e^t>2$

$t>\ln 2\text{ hours}$

$\ln 2\times 60=41.588\cdots$

$t>41.588\cdots\text{ mins}$

$t=42\text{ mins}$

There is an A day every week, except weeks 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36

$\therefore\ P(\text{A})=\dfrac{34}{200}=\dfrac{17}{100}=17\%$

$P(\text{A}\,|\,\text{Monday})=\dfrac{|\text{A}\cap\text{Monday}|}{|\text{Mondays}|}=\dfrac{7}{40}=17.5\%$

Since this is not equal to the answer in part (i), these events are dependent

solutions.latex:
$t=\dfrac{2R\cos\theta}{v_1}+\dfrac{2R\theta}{v_2}$

$\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta+\dfrac{2R}{v_2}$

$\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$ when:

$\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\sin\theta=\dfrac{2R}{v_2}$

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}$

$\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$

$\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}=-\dfrac{2R}{v_1}\cos\theta$

Since $\dfrac{d^2t}{d\theta^2}\le 0$ in the entire domain, $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ is a local maximum.

As this is the only turning point between the end points, the global maximum cannot occur at the end points, thus $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$ gives the global maximum.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Correct angle with justification of maximum; 3: Solves $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}=0$ to get $\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)$; 2: Correct $\dfrac{dt}{d\theta}$; 1: Correct expression for $t$

solutions.latex:
The minimum must occur at the end points $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

When $\theta=0$, $t=\dfrac{2R}{v_1}$

When $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $t=\dfrac{\pi R}{v_2}$

For the minimum to occur by only running, we require $\dfrac{\pi R}{v_2}<\dfrac{2R}{v_1}$

So $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}>\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct condition $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}>\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; 1: Finds $t$ at both end points
